defaults.permitted_development: Across Surrey, a wraparound extension only stays within permitted development if the side and rear elements both satisfy Class A when read together. The combined footprint, leftover garden and mass at the rear corner are often what force the scheme into a full application.

rules.height_rules: Across Surrey, single-storey wraparounds still need to stay within the usual Class A height limits, with particular care on the side return where the 3m eaves rule can bite close to a boundary. The lower the side arm reads, the safer the design usually is.
rules.depth_rules: The rear leg still has to satisfy the normal rear-extension depth rules and the side leg must remain proportionate to the original house. A wraparound cannot borrow generosity from one side of the design to excuse excess on the other.
rules.boundary_rules: Across Surrey, neighbour impact is usually judged at the side boundary and rear corner together. A scheme that looks acceptable in plan can still feel overbearing once those two faces are read as one mass.
rules.roof_rules: Keep the roof quiet and subordinate. The more the roof wraps around as one bulky form, the harder it is to argue that the work remains a modest householder addition.
rules.materials_rules: Materials should match or sit comfortably with the existing house so the side-and-rear combination reads as one coherent addition rather than an oversized add-on.

rules.permitted_development: The wraparound fallback is narrow: both the side return and the rear projection have to satisfy Class A as one combined proposal. In Elmbridge, the practical check is whether the combined footprint still leaves a believable amount of open garden and a side return that does not take over the plot.

rules.height_rules: For height, the familiar Class A envelope still applies, but the side arm is usually the sensitive part because of the 3m eaves rule close to a boundary. rules.depth_rules: The rear leg still has to meet the normal rear-extension depth rules, and the side leg must remain proportionate to the original house. A wraparound layout cannot borrow tolerance from one element to excuse the other.
rules.boundary_rules: With wraparounds, the harder boundary question is usually the combined effect of the side wall and the rear corner when seen from neighbouring gardens. In Elmbridge, neighbour impact is often created by the rear corner and side boundary together rather than by one wall viewed in isolation.
rules.roof_rules: Keep the roof simple and subordinate. Joined-up roofs that create a large boxy mass around the rear corner are more likely to need permission than a clearly secondary arrangement.
rules.materials_rules: External materials should match or sit comfortably with the existing house so the combined side-and-rear form does not look like an overgrown add-on. Councils usually focus on whether the work stays subordinate to the original building and avoids an overbearing effect on neighbours.

restrictions.conservation_area: In a conservation area, a wraparound has to stay visually quiet at the side return and rear corner so the original form of the house still reads clearly.
restrictions.listed_building: Listed buildings do not benefit from the usual wraparound shortcuts; once character is affected, listed building consent is normally central to the route.
